title: Dual Nature of Radiation & Matter
subtitle: Zero-to-JEE-Advanced Visual Textbook: Photon Quantum Theory, Radiation Force & Pressure, Einstein's Photoelectric Equation, Stopping Potential Graphs, de Broglie Matter Waves, Davisson-Germer & Heisenberg Uncertainty Principle
introduction:
💡 First-Time Reader Intuition: Is Light a Wave or a Stream of Particles?

In Chapter 23 (Wave Optics), Young's Double Slit Experiment proved beyond doubt that light behaves as a continuous electromagnetic wave when it propagates, interferes, and diffracts. Yet at the turn of the 20th century, experiments on blackbody radiation and the Photoelectric Effect revealed a shocking paradox: when light interacts with matter (is emitted or absorbed by atoms), it behaves not like a continuous wave, but like a hailstorm of discrete energy packets called Photons!

In 1924, Louis de Broglie completed the symmetry of nature by proposing that if waves (light) can behave like particles, then particles of matter (electrons, protons, atoms) must also behave like waves with wavelength $\lambda = \frac{h}{p}$. This wave-particle duality is the foundation of Quantum Mechanics.

High-Speed JEE Conversion Constants to Memorize:
  • 1 Electron-Volt ($1\text{ eV}$): The kinetic energy gained by an electron accelerated through $1\text{ Volt}$: $$\boxed{1\text{ eV} = 1.6 \times 10^{-19}\text{ J}}$$
  • Planck's Constant ($h$): $h = 6.626 \times 10^{-34}\text{ J}\cdot\text{s} = 4.136 \times 10^{-15}\text{ eV}\cdot\text{s}$.
  • The Golden $hc$ Shortcut: Instead of multiplying $6.63 \times 10^{-34}$ and $3 \times 10^8$ in every exam question, use: $$\boxed{h c \approx 12400\text{ eV}\cdot\text{\AA} = 1240\text{ eV}\cdot\text{nm} \approx 2 \times 10^{-25}\text{ J}\cdot\text{m}}$$

topics.title: Quantum Theory of Light (Photons), Photon Flux, Momentum & Radiation Force/Pressure on Surfaces
topics.theoryHtml:
1.1 Properties of a Photon (Energy, Momentum & Effective Mass)
Planck-Einstein Photon Hypothesis:
A beam of light of frequency $ u$ (and vacuum wavelength $\lambda = c/ u$) consists of discrete quanta called photons. All photons travel in vacuum at the exact speed of light $c = 3 imes 10^8 ext{ m/s}$, are electrically neutral ($q = 0$), and have zero rest mass ($m_0 = 0$).
$$ ext{1. Energy of 1 Photon:} \qquad oxed{E = h u = rac{h c}{\lambda} = rac{12400}{\lambda ext{ (in \AA)}} ext{ eV} = rac{1240}{\lambda ext{ (in nm)}} ext{ eV}}$$
$$ ext{2. Linear Momentum of 1 Photon:} \qquad oxed{p = rac{E}{c} = rac{h u}{c} = rac{h}{\lambda}} \qquad \left( ext{Dynamic Mass } m_{ ext{eff}} = rac{E}{c^2} = rac{h}{c\lambda} ight)$$

Photon Count ($N$) & Photon Flux ($n = rac{dN}{dt}$):
If a monochromatic light source of power $P$ (in Watts) and wavelength $\lambda$ emits $n$ photons per second, and produces intensity $I = rac{P}{A}$ on area $A$:

$$ oxed{n = rac{dN}{dt} = rac{ ext{Power } (P)}{ ext{Energy of 1 Photon } (h c / \lambda)} = rac{P \lambda}{h c} = rac{I A \lambda}{h c}} \qquad \left( ext{For } P = 1 ext{ W}: \; n \approx 5 imes 10^{24} imes \lambda( ext{in m}) ext{ photons/s} ight)$$
1.2 Radiation Force ($F_{ ext{rad}}$) & Radiation Pressure ($P_{ ext{rad}}$)

When a light beam of power $P = I A$ strikes a surface, each absorbed photon transfers momentum $p = rac{h}{\lambda} = rac{E}{c}$, and each reflected photon transfers $2p = rac{2E}{c}$. If a surface has reflection coefficient $r$ and absorption coefficient $a = 1 - r$:

Surface TypeNormal Incidence ($ heta = 0^\circ$)Oblique Incidence at Angle $ heta$ to Normal
1. Completely Absorbing Surface
(Blackbody, $r = 0, a = 1$)		$$ oxed{F = rac{P}{c} = rac{I A}{c}}, \qquad oxed{P_{ ext{rad}} = rac{I}{c}}$$$F_{ ext{along beam}} = rac{I(A\cos heta)}{c}$
$$ oxed{P_{ ext{normal}} = rac{F\cos heta}{A} = rac{I\cos^2 heta}{c}}$$
2. Perfectly Reflecting Mirror
($r = 1, a = 0$)		$$ oxed{F = rac{2P}{c} = rac{2 I A}{c}}, \qquad oxed{P_{ ext{rad}} = rac{2I}{c}}$$$$ oxed{F_{ ext{normal}} = rac{2P\cos heta}{c}}, \qquad oxed{P_{ ext{rad}} = rac{2I\cos^2 heta}{c}}$$
3. Partially Reflecting Surface
(Reflectivity $r$, Absorptivity $1-r$)		$$ oxed{F = (1 + r) rac{P}{c}}, \qquad oxed{P_{ ext{rad}} = (1 + r) rac{I}{c}}$$$$P_{ ext{normal}} = rac{I\cos^2 heta}{c}(1 + r)$$
topics.derivationHtml:
Why Radiation Pressure at Oblique Incidence θ Has a Factor of cos²θ: P_rad = (2I cos²θ) / c

Suppose a parallel light beam of intensity $I$ strikes a flat mirror of area $A$ at angle $ heta$ with the normal. Why are there two factors of $\cos heta$?

Factor 1 (Intercepted Cross-Sectional Area): A tilted surface of area $A$ intercepts a beam cross-section of only $A_{\perp} = A\cos heta$. Thus the power hitting the mirror is $P_{ ext{hit}} = I A_{\perp} = I A \cos heta$, and the number of photons hitting per second is $n = rac{I A \cos heta}{h u}$.

Factor 2 (Normal Momentum Component): Each photon of momentum $p = rac{h u}{c}$ bounces off symmetrically at angle $ heta$, so its normal momentum changes by $\Delta p_{\perp} = 2p\cos heta = rac{2h u\cos heta}{c}$.

Multiplying $n$ by $\Delta p_{\perp}$ and dividing by surface area $A$ gives:

$$F_{\perp} = n \cdot \Delta p_{\perp} = rac{2 I A \cos^2 heta}{c} \implies oxed{P_{ ext{rad}} = rac{F_{\perp}}{A} = rac{2 I \cos^2 heta}{c}}$$

topics.jeeTraps: • Trap (Same Power $P$ of Red Light vs. Violet Light — Which Emits More Photons per Second?): Since $n = \frac{P\lambda}{hc} \propto \lambda$, for the same power $P$ (say $10\text{ W}$), a Red laser ($\lambda \approx 700\text{ nm}$, lower energy per photon) emits MORE photons per second than a Violet laser ($\lambda \approx 400\text{ nm}$, higher energy per photon)! However, both exert the exact same radiation force $F = P/c$ because $F = P/c$ depends only on total power $P$, not on wavelength $\lambda$!

topics.title: Photoelectric Effect: Work Function, Threshold Frequency/Wavelength, Einstein's Equation, Stopping Potential & All 4 Experimental Graphs
topics.theoryHtml:
2.1 Work Function ($\phi_0$), Thresholds & Einstein's Photoelectric Equation
Work Function ($\phi_0$ or $W_0$):
The minimum energy required by the most loosely bound conduction electron to just escape from the metal surface against attractive surface forces. It is a pure property of the metal material (lowest for Alkali metals: Cesium $ ext{Cs}$ has $\phi_0 \approx 2.14 ext{ eV}$; highest for Platinum $ ext{Pt}$ with $\phi_0 \approx 5.65 ext{ eV}$).
$$ ext{Work Function:} \qquad oxed{\phi_0 = h u_0 = rac{h c}{\lambda_0} = rac{12400}{\lambda_0 ext{ (in \AA)}} ext{ eV}}$$

For photoelectric emission to occur, incident light must have $ oxed{ u \ge u_0}$ (Threshold Frequency) or equivalently $ oxed{\lambda \le \lambda_0}$ (Threshold / Cut-off Wavelength)!

Einstein's Photoelectric Equation (1905 Nobel Prize):
Photoelectric emission is an instantaneous ($\sim 10^{-9} ext{ s}$) one-to-one elastic collision between 1 incident photon (energy $h u$) and 1 electron inside the metal. Because most electrons lose some energy in internal collisions before reaching the surface, emitted photoelectrons have kinetic energies ranging from $0$ up to a sharp maximum $K_{\max}$:
$$ oxed{K_{\max} = rac{1}{2}m v_{\max}^2 = h u - \phi_0 = h( u - u_0) = h c\left( rac{1}{\lambda} - rac{1}{\lambda_0} ight)}$$

Stopping Potential (Cut-off Voltage $V_s$ or $V_0$):
The minimum negative (retarding) potential applied to the collector plate with respect to the emitter that stops even the fastest photoelectron ($K_{\max}$) from reaching the collector ($I_{ ext{photo}} = 0$):

$$ oxed{e V_s = K_{\max} = h u - \phi_0 \implies V_s = \left( rac{h}{e} ight) u - rac{\phi_0}{e}}$$
2.2 Master Table of Intensity ($I$) vs. Frequency ($ u$) Effects in Photoelectric Experiment
Experimental Change (Assuming $ u > u_0$)Effect on Saturation Photocurrent ($I_{ ext{sat}}$)Effect on $K_{\max}$ & Stopping Potential ($V_s$)
1. Increase Intensity $I$ (Keep $ u$ constant)
(e.g., move point source closer: $I \propto 1/r^2$)		Increases proportionally ($I_{ ext{sat}} \propto I$)!
(More photons/s $\implies$ more photoelectrons/s).		100% UNCHANGED!
($K_{\max}$ and $V_s$ depend ONLY on $ u$ and $\phi_0$).
2. Increase Frequency $ u$ (Keep photon flux constant)Remains constant (or decreases slightly if total power $P = n h u$ is kept constant, since $n = P/(h u)$ drops!).Increases linearly!
(Notice: doubling $ u$ from $ u$ to $2 u$ makes $K_{\max}' = 2h u - \phi_0 = 2K_{\max} + \phi_0 > 2K_{\max}$, i.e., MORE than double!).

Universal Slope of $V_s$ vs. $ u$ Graph: For EVERY metal in the universe, the graph of Stopping Potential $V_s$ vs. Frequency $ u$ is a straight line with identical universal slope $ oxed{ an heta = rac{h}{e} \approx 4.14 imes 10^{-15} ext{ V}\cdot ext{s}}$ (while the slope of $K_{\max}$ vs. $ u$ is simply Planck's constant $h$)!
topics.derivationHtml:
Why Classical Wave Theory Completely Failed to Explain the Photoelectric Effect (3 Fatal Contradictions)

1. Intensity Problem: In classical wave theory, higher intensity $I = \frac{1}{2}\varepsilon_0 c E_0^2$ means a stronger electric field $E_0$, which should shake electrons harder and increase $K_{\max}$. In reality, $K_{\max}$ is 100% independent of intensity $I$!

2. Threshold Frequency Problem: Classical wave theory predicts that light of ANY frequency should eject electrons if it is bright enough. In reality, below $\nu_0$, even a blinding laser beam ejects ZERO electrons!

3. Time-Lag Problem: Classical wave theory spreads energy uniformly across the wavefront, so a single atom would take hours to soak up enough energy $\phi_0$ from a dim light beam. In reality, emission is instantaneous ($< 10^{-9}\text{ s}$) because 1 photon delivers its entire $h\nu$ packet to 1 electron at once!

topics.jeeTraps:
• Trap 1 (Polychromatic / Dichromatic Light Hitting a Metal Surface): If a light beam containing three wavelengths $\lambda_1 = 3000\text{ \AA}$, $\lambda_2 = 4000\text{ \AA}$, and $\lambda_3 = 6000\text{ \AA}$ illuminates a metal plate, the stopping potential $V_s$ of the plate is decided exclusively by the highest-frequency (shortest-wavelength $\lambda_1 = 3000\text{ \AA}$) photons: $eV_s = \frac{hc}{\lambda_{\min}} - \phi_0$!
  • Trap 2 (Isolated Metallic Sphere Illuminated by UV Light): As an isolated uncharged conducting sphere of radius $R$ emits photoelectrons, it acquires a positive charge $+Q$ and positive potential $V = \frac{kQ}{R}$. Emission stops automatically when the sphere's potential reaches the stopping potential: $\boxed{\frac{k Q_{\max}}{R} = V_s = \frac{h\nu - \phi_0}{e}}$!

topics.title: de Broglie Matter Waves, Accelerating Voltage Shortcuts, Davisson-Germer Experiment & Heisenberg's Uncertainty Principle
topics.theoryHtml:
3.1 de Broglie Wavelength of Matter Particles ($\lambda = h/p$)
de Broglie Hypothesis (1924):
Every moving material particle having linear momentum $p = mv$ has an associated matter wave (pilot wave) of wavelength $\lambda$:
$$\boxed{\lambda = \frac{h}{p} = \frac{h}{m v} = \frac{h}{\sqrt{2 m K}} = \frac{h}{\sqrt{2 m q V_{\text{acc}}}}}$$

Numerical Shortcuts for Particles Accelerated Through Potential Difference $V$ (in Volts) to Memorize:

ParticleMass & Chargede Broglie Wavelength $\lambda$ (in Angstroms $\text{\AA} = 10^{-10}\text{ m}$)
1. Electron ($e^-$)$m_e, \; q = e$$$\boxed{\lambda_e = \sqrt{\frac{150}{V}}\text{ \AA} \approx \frac{12.27}{\sqrt{V}}\text{ \AA}}$$
2. Proton ($p$ / ${}_1^1\text{H}$)$m_p \approx 1836\,m_e, \; q = e$$$\boxed{\lambda_p = \frac{0.286}{\sqrt{V}}\text{ \AA}}$$
3. Deuteron ($d$ / ${}_1^2\text{H}$)$m_d = 2m_p, \; q = e$$$\boxed{\lambda_d = \frac{0.202}{\sqrt{V}}\text{ \AA}}$$
4. Alpha Particle ($\alpha$ / ${}_2^4\text{He}^{2+}$)$m_\alpha = 4m_p, \; q = 2e$$$\boxed{\lambda_\alpha = \frac{0.101}{\sqrt{V}}\text{ \AA}}$$
5. Thermal Neutron / Gas Molecule at Temp $T$$K_{\text{avg}} = \frac{3}{2}k_B T$ (or $k_B T$)$$\boxed{\lambda_{\text{thermal}} = \frac{h}{\sqrt{3 m k_B T}}} \quad \left(\text{For neutron at } 300\text{ K: } \lambda \approx 1.45\text{ \AA}\right)$$
3.2 Davisson-Germer Electron Diffraction Experiment & Heisenberg's Uncertainty Principle
  • Davisson-Germer Experiment (1927): Confirmed the wave nature of electrons by diffracting a low-energy electron beam off a Nickel ($\text{Ni}$) crystal ($d = 0.91\text{ \AA}$). A strong constructive diffraction peak was observed at accelerating voltage $\boxed{V = 54\text{ Volts}}$ and scattering angle $\boxed{\phi = 50^\circ}$ (giving $\lambda = \frac{12.27}{\sqrt{54}} = \mathbf{1.67\text{ \AA}}$, matching Bragg's law $2D\sin\theta = \lambda$!).
  • Heisenberg's Uncertainty Principle: It is fundamentally impossible to measure both the exact position $x$ and exact momentum $p_x$ (or energy $E$ and time $t$) of a quantum particle simultaneously with arbitrary precision:
    $$\boxed{\Delta x \cdot \Delta p_x \ge \frac{h}{4\pi} = \frac{\hbar}{2}} \qquad \text{and} \qquad \boxed{\Delta E \cdot \Delta t \ge \frac{h}{4\pi} = \frac{\hbar}{2}} \qquad \left(\text{where } \hbar = \frac{h}{2\pi} = 1.054 \times 10^{-34}\text{ J}\cdot\text{s}\right)$$
topics.derivationHtml:
de Broglie Wavelength of a Particle Moving in an Electric Field E(t) Starting from Velocity v₀

Suppose a particle of mass $m$ and charge $q$ has initial velocity $\vec{v} = v_0\hat{i}$ and is subjected to a uniform electric field $\vec{E} = E_0\hat{j}$. At time $t$, its velocity vector is $\vec{v}(t) = v_0\hat{i} + \left(\frac{qE_0 t}{m}\right)\hat{j}$, so the magnitude of its momentum is $p(t) = m|\vec{v}(t)| = \sqrt{m^2 v_0^2 + q^2 E_0^2 t^2}$. Therefore, its instantaneous de Broglie wavelength is:

$$\boxed{\lambda(t) = \frac{h}{p(t)} = \frac{h}{\sqrt{m^2 v_0^2 + q^2 E_0^2 t^2}} = \frac{\lambda_0}{\sqrt{1 + \frac{q^2 E_0^2 t^2}{m^2 v_0^2}}}}$$

topics.jeeTraps:
• Trap 1 (Photon vs. Electron with the Same Wavelength $\lambda$ — Which Has Greater Energy?): Since both have the exact same wavelength $\lambda$, their momenta are identical ($p_{\text{photon}} = p_e = \frac{h}{\lambda}$)! However, their kinetic energies are $E_{\text{photon}} = p c$ and $K_e = \frac{p^2}{2m_e} = \frac{1}{2}p v_e$. Since $v_e \ll c$, the photon has much GREATER energy than the electron ($\frac{E_{\text{photon}}}{K_e} = \frac{2c}{v_e} \gg 1$)!
  • Trap 2 (Do Matter Waves Travel at the Speed of Light $c$? NO!): Matter waves are NOT electromagnetic waves! They do not require a charge (neutrons have matter waves too), and the wave packet (group velocity) of a matter wave travels at the particle's own physical velocity $v < c$!

conclusion: You have mastered Chapter 24: Dual Nature of Radiation & Matter! Next, in Chapter 25, we apply photons and de Broglie standing waves to the structure of the Atom and X-ray spectra.
summary:
• Photons & Radiation Force: $E = h u = rac{hc}{\lambda} = rac{12400}{\lambda( ext{\AA})} ext{ eV}$, $p = rac{h}{\lambda}$; Radiation pressure $P_{ ext{rad}} = (1 + r) rac{I}{c}\cos^2 heta$.
  • Photoelectric Effect: $K_{\max} = eV_s = h u - \phi_0 = hc\left( rac{1}{\lambda} - rac{1}{\lambda_0} ight)$; $I_{ ext{sat}} \propto ext{Intensity}$; $V_s$ depends only on $ u$.
  • de Broglie Waves: $\lambda = rac{h}{p} = rac{h}{\sqrt{2mK}} = rac{h}{\sqrt{2mqV}}$; Electron $\lambda_e = \sqrt{ rac{150}{V}} ext{ \AA} \approx rac{12.27}{\sqrt{V}} ext{ \AA}$.
  • Uncertainty Principle: $\Delta x \cdot \Delta p \ge rac{h}{4\pi}$ and $\Delta E \cdot \Delta t \ge rac{h}{4\pi}$.

ConceptMaster FormulaKey Notes
Photon Energy & Flux$E = \dfrac{12400}{\lambda(\text{\AA})}\text{ eV}, \qquad n = \dfrac{P\lambda}{hc}$$hc \approx 12400\text{ eV}\cdot\text{\AA} = 1240\text{ eV}\cdot\text{nm}$.

questions.prompt: Monochromatic light of wavelength $\lambda = 3100\text{ \AA}$ falls on a metal surface whose work function is $\phi_0 = 2.5\text{ eV}$. What is the stopping potential $V_s$ for the emitted photoelectrons? (Use $hc = 12400\text{ eV}\cdot\text{\AA}$)
questions.explanation: Energy of each incident photon is $E = \frac{12400}{3100}\text{ eV} = 4.0\text{ eV}$. Therefore, $K_{\max} = E - \phi_0 = 4.0 - 2.5 = 1.5\text{ eV}$, which gives stopping potential $V_s = 1.5\text{ V}$.

questions.prompt: What is the de Broglie wavelength $\lambda$ of an electron accelerated from rest through a potential difference of $V = 100\text{ Volts}$?
questions.explanation: Using the electron de Broglie formula $\lambda = \frac{12.27}{\sqrt{V}}\text{ \AA} = \frac{12.27}{\sqrt{100}} = 1.227\text{ \AA}$.

questions.prompt: When a metallic surface is illuminated with radiation of wavelength $\lambda$, the stopping potential is $V_0$. If the same surface is illuminated with radiation of wavelength $2\lambda$, the stopping potential drops to $\frac{V_0}{4}$. What is the threshold wavelength $\lambda_0$ for this metallic surface?
questions.explanation: We have $eV_0 = \frac{hc}{\lambda} - \frac{hc}{\lambda_0}$ and $\frac{eV_0}{4} = \frac{hc}{2\lambda} - \frac{hc}{\lambda_0}$. Multiplying the second equation by $4$ and equating to the first: $\frac{hc}{\lambda} - \frac{hc}{\lambda_0} = \frac{2hc}{\lambda} - \frac{4hc}{\lambda_0} \implies \frac{3hc}{\lambda_0} = \frac{hc}{\lambda} \implies \lambda_0 = 3\lambda$.

questions.prompt: A proton ($m_p, +e$) and an alpha particle ($4m_p, +2e$) are accelerated from rest through the same potential difference $V$. The ratio of their de Broglie wavelengths ($\lambda_p : \lambda_\alpha$) is:
questions.explanation: Since $\lambda = \frac{h}{\sqrt{2mqV}} \propto \frac{1}{\sqrt{mq}}$ at the same voltage $V$, we get $\frac{\lambda_p}{\lambda_\alpha} = \sqrt{\frac{m_\alpha q_\alpha}{m_p q_p}} = \sqrt{\frac{(4m_p)(2e)}{m_p e}} = \sqrt{8} = 2\sqrt{2} : 1$.

questions.prompt: A laser beam of power $P = 30\text{ mW}$ strikes a plane mirror at an angle of incidence $\theta = 60^\circ$ to the normal and is $100\%$ reflected. What is the magnitude of the radiation force exerted by the laser beam on the mirror? ($c = 3 \times 10^8\text{ m/s}$)
questions.explanation: For $100\%$ reflection at incidence angle $\theta = 60^\circ$, the normal force is $F = \frac{2P\cos\theta}{c} = \frac{2(30 \times 10^{-3}\text{ W})\cos 60^\circ}{3 \times 10^8\text{ m/s}} = \frac{2 \times 0.03 \times 0.5}{3 \times 10^8} = 1.0 \times 10^{-10}\text{ N}$.

questions.prompt: An isolated, initially uncharged metallic sphere of radius $R = 9\text{ mm}$ is suspended in vacuum and illuminated with ultraviolet light of wavelength $\lambda = 2000\text{ \AA}$. If the work function of the sphere metal is $\phi_0 = 4.7\text{ eV}$, what is the maximum number of photoelectrons that can be emitted from the sphere before photoelectric emission stops completely? (Use $hc = 12400\text{ eV}\cdot\text{\AA}$ and $\frac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_0} = 9 \times 10^9\text{ N}\cdot\text{m}^2/\text{C}^2$)
questions.explanation: Photon energy $E = \frac{12400}{2000} = 6.2\text{ eV}$. Thus $K_{\max} = 6.2 - 4.7 = 1.5\text{ eV}$, and stopping potential is $V_s = 1.5\text{ V}$. Emission stops when the sphere's potential reaches $V = \frac{k(N e)}{R} = V_s = 1.5\text{ V} \implies N = \frac{V_s R}{k e} = \frac{(1.5)(9 \times 10^{-3})}{(9 \times 10^9)(1.6 \times 10^{-19})} = \frac{1.5}{1.6} \times 10^7 = 9.375 \times 10^6\text{ electrons}$.
